Q: PowerShell Class Inheritance from separate file using Import-Module A:

The accepted answer is correct — using module is the right tool here. To understand why Import-Module doesn't work for class inheritance: PowerShell resolves class definitions at parse time, but Import-Module runs at runtime. By the time bar is parsed, foo doesn't exist yet, so the class is created without the inherited members — the error only surfaces when you call a method.

using module is processed before the file is compiled, which is why it works.

The next problem — scaling

Once you have more than a handful of classes, the using module approach becomes harder to maintain. Every file must declare its own dependencies explicitly, and with complex inheritance trees — properties, method parameters, return types — keeping all references consistent across many files becomes error-prone.

The more robust approach for larger projects is a build step that compiles all source files into a single .psm1 in the correct dependency order:

# Build.ps1 — compile into a single .psm1
$outputPath = '.\output\MyModule.psm1'
$null = New-Item -Path $outputPath -Force

# Base classes first
Get-Content '.\src\foo.ps1' | Add-Content $outputPath

# Then derived classes
Get-Content '.\src\bar.ps1' | Add-Content $outputPath

The compiled .psm1 contains all classes in one file — no using module chains needed. This works well for small projects, but the file list must be maintained manually. Every time you add a class or change an inheritance relationship, the build script needs updating — and a wrong order breaks the module at parse time with a hard-to-diagnose error.

Automating this is exactly the problem PSScriptBuilder was built to solve. It uses the PowerShell AST to analyze inheritance and type references across all source files and determines the correct compile order automatically.

Disclosure: I am the author of PSScriptBuilder.

Q: Package Manager Console is not showing A:

After you select menu Tools → Nuget Package Manager → Package Manager Console, even if the window cannot be seen, Visual Studio 2022 should be in the "selected" state for this window.

Therefore, "Window" Settings on the top of the Visual Studio 2022 will be able to control the current Package Manager Console window. Please try to open the Package Manager Console and then click menu Window → Dock as tabbed Document. This setting will maximize the Package Manager Console window:

Q: How can I generate many random community matrices and then apply a function to all of them? A:

If you want to find Mean Phylogenetic Distance (MPD) or Mean Nearest Taxon Distance (MNTD), you can use package picante.

ses.mpd(comm, phy.dist, null.model = "richness", abundance.weighted = FALSE, runs = 999)

The runs comand is the number of random communities generated.
